passage: In the village school near Moga, the new teacher, Nirmala Ma'am, held out a choice to each child who had finished the reading chart: one toffee now, or a real storybook next Friday. Most children picked the book. Gurpreet grabbed the toffee at once and put it in her pocket. Ma'am tilted her head. "You love stories, Gurpreet." Gurpreet looked at the floor. Last year the other teacher had promised a picnic and it never happened. Her Chacha promised a cycle every Diwali. The fair Papa said they'd go to, twice, never came either. "Next Friday might not come," she mumbled. That Friday, Ma'am handed out the books. She also quietly put one on Gurpreet's desk. Gurpreet stared at it, then at Ma'am, for a long time.

qa.q: What choice did Nirmala Ma'am offer the children?
qa.a: One toffee now, or a real storybook next Friday.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet grab the toffee even though she loves stories?
qa.a: So many adult promises had been broken, the picnic, the cycle, the fair, that a later reward felt unlikely, so taking one now made sense to her.

qa.q: What choice did Nirmala Ma'am make on Friday, and why might it matter?
qa.a: She quietly gave Gurpreet a book anyway, showing this adult's promises can be trusted, which may make waiting feel possible next time.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Ma'am understand Gurpreet's choice after hearing 'Next Friday might not come'?
qa.a: She seems to see it not as greed or weak character but as a sensible choice by a child who has been let down before.

grounding: A village girl let down by adults' promises takes the small reward now, a reasonable choice when the future feels unreliable.

passage: Elif had lived with Vera in Hamburg for only three weeks, after two other foster homes. On Thursday Vera said, "We can get a small ice cream now, or save the money and go to the zoo on Saturday. Your choice." Elif said, "Ice cream now," before Vera finished the sentence. She ate it fast on the bench, watching Vera the whole time. Vera didn't argue. That night Vera wrote "ZOO, SATURDAY" on the kitchen calendar in big green letters. On Friday she showed Elif the tickets on her phone. On Saturday they went. Elif walked past the penguins quietly, holding the ticket stub tight. The next week, when Vera offered a choice again, Elif hesitated. "Maybe... the later one?"

qa.q: What did Vera write on the kitchen calendar?
qa.a: "ZOO, SATURDAY", in big green letters.

qa.q: Why did Elif choose ice cream before Vera even finished?
qa.a: After two other foster homes, promises about Saturday may have seemed unreliable, so taking the sure thing now felt safer.

qa.q: What did Vera choose to do instead of arguing, and why did it help?
qa.a: She kept the promise in visible steps, the calendar, the tickets, the trip, which slowly gave Elif a reason to trust a later reward.

qa.q: What might Elif's hesitation the next week mean to Vera?
qa.a: Vera may feel quietly hopeful, seeing that one kept promise has started to change what Elif expects.

grounding: A girl in foster care grabs the immediate treat because promises have been unreliable, and a kept promise begins to change that.

passage: At the girls' hostel in Siliguri, Bidisha didi, the warden, ran a token system: one token bought a biscuit packet on Monday, or three tokens saved till Sunday bought a trip to the river. Most girls saved. Nazia spent hers the moment she got them, every single time. The older girls called her greedy. Bidisha didi watched for a few weeks. Then she looked at Nazia's file: the girl had moved hostels three times, and two promised home visits had been cancelled. That evening she sat with Nazia on the steps. "You think Sunday won't happen?" Nazia shrugged. "Things get cancelled." Bidisha didi nodded. "That makes sense. This Sunday I'll take you myself, tokens or no tokens. Then you decide."

qa.q: What could three tokens saved till Sunday buy?
qa.a: A trip to the river.

qa.q: Why did Nazia spend her tokens the moment she got them?
qa.a: After moving hostels three times and having home visits cancelled, she didn't trust that Sunday would really come, so using them now felt safe.

qa.q: What choice did Bidisha didi make after reading the file, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She named Nazia's reason kindly and promised to take her on Sunday regardless, so Nazia can see a promise kept before being asked to wait.

qa.q: How did the older girls see Nazia, and what were they missing?
qa.a: They called her greedy, missing that her quick spending came from broken promises, not weak character.

grounding: In a hostel, a girl who has seen promises broken spends rewards at once, and the warden treats it as reasonable rather than greedy.

passage: I'm Keerthana, and I live in the flat opposite Ayesha's. Last Saturday our building held a drawing contest for the little ones. Ravi Uncle, the secretary, said, "Winners can take one chocolate now, or wait till Diwali for a big box of colours." Every other child said Diwali. Ayesha, who's nine, took the chocolate before he'd finished the sentence and ate it on the spot. Some aunties tutted. But I've heard things through the wall. Her father promised the zoo, then the beach, then a new school bag, and none of it happened. When I sat next to her on the stairs, she said, "Diwali is far. Things change." She didn't look greedy to me. She looked like someone who'd stopped counting on later.

qa.q: What were the contest winners offered?
qa.a: One chocolate now, or wait till Diwali for a big box of colours.

qa.q: Why did grabbing the chocolate feel sensible to Ayesha?
qa.a: Ayesha feels wary and distrustful of 'later', because her father's promises of the zoo, the beach and a school bag never happened; a chocolate now is the only sure thing.

qa.q: What could the adults around Ayesha do to change what she expects from waiting?
qa.a: Keep small promises to her reliably, starting with short waits, so that later begins to feel real; tutting at her won't teach that.

qa.q: Why might Keerthana see Ayesha differently from the aunties who tutted?
qa.a: Keerthana has heard the broken promises through the wall, so Keerthana reads the grab as wariness learned at home rather than greed.

grounding: A neighbour sees a child who has learned that adult promises fail grab the reward at once, and reads it as reasonable rather than greedy.

passage:
First week at the hostel: Hemant, ten, got a choice from Omkar Sir, the new warden: one packet of peanuts now, or two on Sunday if his room stayed tidy. Hemant snatched the peanuts. "Sunday never comes," he muttered. At home, his uncle's "next week" had always meant never.
Third week: Omkar Sir said, "Help me paint the notice board on Friday, and on Saturday we'll fly your kite." On Saturday, under a grey sky, they flew it from the terrace. Hemant kept glancing at him, as if waiting for a catch.
Sixth week: Offered peanuts now or a cricket match on Sunday, Hemant chose Sunday. He still crossed the days off the calendar every night.

qa.q: What did Hemant choose in the sixth week?
qa.a: Hemant chose the cricket match on Sunday.

qa.q: Why did Hemant keep glancing at Omkar Sir during the kite flying?
qa.a: He half expected the good thing to fall apart, as his uncle's 'next week' always had; trust was growing, but he was still watching for a catch.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Hemant's choices?
qa.a: Omkar Sir flying the kite on Saturday exactly as promised; that kept word showed Hemant that later could be real, and by the sixth week he chose to wait.

qa.q: How might Omkar Sir have read the peanut-snatching in the first week?
qa.a: A thoughtful warden would see caution learned from broken promises rather than greed, which fits Omkar Sir answering with kept promises instead of scolding.

grounding: A child used to broken promises grabs the reward at once, which makes sense until a reliable adult makes waiting worthwhile.
